specPoints.text: understand how the pitch of a sound relates to the frequency of vibration of the source
understand how the loudness of a sound relates to the amplitude of vibration of the source
know that the frequency range for human hearing is 20–20 000 Hz

primer.text: Pitch and loudness are the two handles a listener has on any note, and both have a mechanical counterpart in the vibrating source. This note fixes the pitch-frequency pairing on the oscilloscope, the loudness-amplitude pairing beside it, and marks out the frequency window of human hearing with its infrasound and ultrasound borders.

lessons.title: Pitch and the oscilloscope trace
sourceHeadings: The relationship between the pitch and frequency of sound
Comparing the pitch of sound displayed on an oscilloscope
lessons.opening: Pitch tracks how fast a sound source vibrates. On an oscilloscope that speed becomes visible as the number of complete cycles packed across the screen, so two notes can be ranked by pitch from their traces alone, without hearing either one.
keyPoints: Pitch tracks the frequency of the vibrating source.
High-frequency vibration gives high pitch and low-frequency vibration gives low pitch.
On an oscilloscope, a higher-frequency note shows more complete cycles across the same screen width.
Wider peak-to-peak spacing on the screen means fewer cycles per second, so lower pitch.
Doubling the frequency of a note raises it by one octave.

low.restatement: Frequency sets pitch; the oscilloscope displays frequency horizontally, so more cycles across the same width is the higher-pitched note.
low.analogy: A garden swing: how many full swings it makes each second is the frequency, and that count is the pitch you hear.
low.examPointer: Octave arithmetic is fair game: doubling frequency (256 → 512 Hz) is one octave up; halving is one octave down.

medium.restatement: Frequency and pitch move together because the ear follows the source’s vibration rate; on screen the comparison is horizontal (cycles per width) while amplitude stays vertical, so pitch and loudness are read from the same trace without confusion.
medium.analogy: Two garden swings of different lengths: the shorter one completes more swings each minute, like the higher-pitched note.
medium.examPointer: Octave arithmetic: doubling the frequency (256 → 512 Hz) raises the note one octave; halving lowers it one octave.

check.stem: Which property of the vibrating source sets the pitch of a sound?

options.explanation: Amplitude sets loudness, not pitch.
Pitch is related to the frequency of the vibrating source.

options.text: the speed of sound in air
options.explanation: Sound speed is the same for all pitches in the same medium.
Distance changes loudness, not pitch.

check.stem: A guitar string is tightened so it vibrates with higher frequency. What happens to the note?

options.explanation: Loudness tracks amplitude, not frequency.
Higher vibration frequency gives higher pitch.
That would need a LOWER frequency.
Guitar strings sit inside the audible range.

check.stem: On an oscilloscope, which feature signals the higher-pitched of two notes?

options.explanation: Height signals loudness.

options.text: more complete waves across the same width
options.explanation: More cycles in the same time window means higher frequency and pitch.
Wider spacing means fewer cycles per second, so LOWER pitch.
Brightness carries no waveform information.

check.stem: A note of frequency 512 Hz sounds beside a 256 Hz note. How do their pitches compare?

options.explanation: Higher frequency means higher pitch; 256 Hz is the lower one.

options.text: the 512 Hz fork sounds one octave above the 256 Hz fork
options.explanation: Doubling the frequency raises the note by one octave, and 512 = 2 × 256.
Different frequencies give different pitches.
The label gives frequency, not amplitude.

check.stem: A violinist plays a note, then a second note one octave higher. The first note had frequency 220 Hz. What was the second note’s frequency?

options.explanation: Halving goes one octave DOWN.
An octave doubles the frequency; 330 is not a doubling.
One octave up doubles the frequency: 2 × 220 = 440 Hz.
The same frequency is the same pitch.

check.stem: State how pitch tracks the vibration of its source.
check.modelAnswer: Pitch tracks the frequency of the vibrating source: high-frequency vibration gives high pitch and low-frequency vibration gives low pitch.

check.stem: Two traces share the same screen width; trace A shows three complete cycles and trace B shows one. State which trace has the lower frequency.
check.modelAnswer: Trace B has the lower frequency, because fewer complete cycles across the same width means fewer cycles per second.

check.stem: Two traces on an oscilloscope have the same height but trace B shows twice as many cycles as trace A across the same width. Explain which is higher-pitched and whether their loudnesses can be told apart.
check.modelAnswer: Trace B completes twice as many cycles in the same time, so its frequency is double and its pitch is higher. Both traces have the same height, so their amplitudes are equal and the oscilloscope gives no loudness difference between them.

check.stem: A mosquito deterrent emits a 17 000 Hz tone. Explain whether a person with full human hearing will hear it, and compare its pitch with a 500 Hz hum.
check.modelAnswer: 17 000 Hz lies below the 20 000 Hz upper limit of human hearing, so a person with full hearing can hear it; it has a much higher frequency than a 500 Hz hum, so it sounds far higher in pitch.

lessons.title: Loudness and the range of human hearing
sourceHeadings: Comparing the volume of sound displayed on an oscilloscope
The infrasound, human hearing and ultrasound frequency ranges
lessons.opening: Loudness tracks how far the source vibrates, and the oscilloscope shows it as trace height. Frequency itself has hard borders for the human ear: 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz, with infrasound below and ultrasound above — a sorting rule examiners love to test.
keyPoints: Loudness tracks the amplitude of the vibrating source: louder sounds swing with larger amplitude.
On an oscilloscope, a louder note shows a taller trace measured from the centre line.
The human ear responds to vibrations caused by sound waves.
Human hearing spans 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.
Frequencies below the range are infrasound and frequencies above it are ultrasound.

low.restatement: Amplitude sets loudness and shows vertically on the screen; frequency has an audible window of 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz, with infrasound underneath and ultrasound above.
low.analogy: A radio that only tunes between two stations: infrasound and ultrasound broadcast outside the dial, perfectly real but unheard.
low.examPointer: Quote the hearing range with units every time: 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz. Sorting a frequency into infra-, audible or ultra- is a one-mark giveaway.

medium.restatement: Loudness scales with amplitude as height on the screen; the 20 Hz–20 000 Hz window then sorts every frequency into audible, infrasound (below) or ultrasound (above), independent of loudness.
medium.analogy: A torch beam too dim to see is still light; an ultrasound tone too high to hear is still sound — the window, not the wave, decides perception.
medium.examPointer: Classification turns on the numbers: 16 Hz < 20 Hz is infrasound, 25 000 Hz > 20 000 Hz is ultrasound; quote the boundary in the answer.

check.stem: A drum is struck harder, so its skin vibrates with larger amplitude. What happens to the sound?

options.explanation: Amplitude does not set pitch.
Larger vibration amplitude gives a louder sound.
Harder strikes change amplitude; frequency is set by the skin’s tension and size.
A drum remains far below 20 000 Hz.

check.stem: What is the frequency range for human hearing?

options.explanation: This is the stated range of human hearing.
Both boundaries are ten times too small.
Both boundaries are ten times too large.
The upper boundary is far too large.

check.stem: A bat emits a 45 000 Hz squeak. How is that sound classified for humans?

options.explanation: Audibility depends on frequency, not loudness.

options.text: ultrasound, because 45 000 Hz is above the human upper limit
options.explanation: 45 000 Hz exceeds 20 000 Hz, so it is ultrasound.
Infrasound is BELOW 20 Hz.

options.text: audible, because 45 000 Hz is below 20 000 Hz
options.explanation: 45 000 is greater than 20 000.

check.stem: An earthquake sensor records a 16 Hz vibration. For human hearing this is:

options.explanation: 16 Hz is below the range, not above.

options.text: infrasound, because it lies below 20 Hz
options.explanation: 16 Hz falls under the 20 Hz lower boundary.
Loudness cannot bring a frequency into range.

options.text: at the centre of the audible range
options.explanation: The centre is near 10 000 Hz.

check.stem: A dog whistle claims 25 000 Hz. Which row is correct for a human and a dog with hearing up to 45 000 Hz?

options.explanation: 25 000 Hz exceeds the human upper limit.
The dog’s limit of 45 000 Hz covers 25 000 Hz.

options.text: the human may hear it and the dog does not
options.explanation: This reverses the two limits.

options.text: the human does not hear it but the dog may
options.explanation: 25 000 Hz is above 20 000 Hz but below the dog’s 45 000 Hz limit.

check.stem: State how loudness tracks the vibration of its source.
check.modelAnswer: Loudness tracks the amplitude of the vibrating source: larger amplitude gives a louder sound.

check.stem: State the names given to sound frequencies below and above the range of human hearing.
check.modelAnswer: Below the range is infrasound and above the range is ultrasound.

check.stem: Explain why a 30 000 Hz dog whistle is silent to a person with full human hearing even when it is blown loudly.
check.modelAnswer: The ear only responds to vibrations between 20 Hz and 20 000 Hz; 30 000 Hz lies above that window, so the eardrum and ear cannot respond to it and no loudness makes it audible.

check.stem: Sort these four frequencies into infrasound, audible and ultrasound: 15 Hz, 440 Hz, 15 000 Hz, 25 000 Hz.
check.modelAnswer: 15 Hz is infrasound because it is below 20 Hz; 440 Hz and 15 000 Hz are audible because both lie between 20 Hz and 20 000 Hz; 25 000 Hz is ultrasound because it is above 20 000 Hz.

glossary.definition: How high or low a sound seems, set by the frequency of the vibrating source.
How strong a sound seems, set by the amplitude of the vibrating source.
Sound with frequency below 20 Hz, outside human hearing.
Sound with frequency above 20 000 Hz, outside human hearing.
